newsitem.title: USA: Silicon Graphics sees Q2 revs $825 mln.
newsitem.headline: Silicon Graphics sees Q2 revs $825 mln.

text.p: Silicon Graphics Inc Monday said it expects revenues for the second quarter ended in December to be around $825 million, down from pro forma revenues of $899 million in the same period last year.
In a statement, issued after the market had closed, the company said it expects net earnings per share to be in the break-even range.

Silicon Graphics executives said the expected break-even figure will be prior to merger charges related to its June 1996 acquisition of supercomputer maker Cray Research Inc., which are expected to amount to $0.08 a share and which the company said are generally not included in analyst estimates.
Wall Street analysts had been expecting the struggling maker of graphics-intensive workstations to report a profit of $0.24 a share, according to a First Call estimate consensus.
The shortfall follows a string of profit warnings dating back to its year-ago second quarter and analysts noted the company is undergoing a huge transition to new products.

Although the company on October 7 introduced its most sweeping new products launch in decades, executives said some of the products had not been shipped until fairly late in the second quarter and that it may take another quarter to complete its "ramp-up" as production reaches full-speed.

Nevertheless, analysts and company executives said a silver lining in the news is the fact the company's backlog at the end of the quarter on December 31, 1996, hit record levels of around $750 million, boosted by demand for the new models.
This compares with $474 million at the end of its first fiscal quarter on September 30, before the product launch.

Although some Wall Street investors will certainly take the latest profit warning as justification for a wait-and-see attitude -- the stock fell to as low as 25-1/4 in after-hours trading after having closed at 26-7/8 prior to the profit warning news -- some hailed the strong backlog as bullish. "Obviously the stock has moved up in the belief they had seen the worst and had headed upward," said Robert Herwick, who heads Herwick Capital Management, noting the share had come back after hitting a 52-week trading low of 17-7/8.
"That's going to happen, but there's this one more hiccup -- it takes time," he added.
Product bookings for the quarter were approximately $950 million, also the highest in the company's history.

Silicon Graphics said it "attributied the strong growth to strong customer acceptance of the new products...including the entry-level O2 workstation and the Origin family of servers, and continued strong demand for Cray Research supercomputers."

Bill Kelly, a senior vice president and general manager of the company's Silicon Interactive unit, said the company had shipped 10,000 of its O2 workstations in the quarter, and was experiencing strong demand and a strong critical reception.
